'''''Populus'' × ''canescens''''', the '''grey poplar''', is a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Populus alba]]'' (white poplar) and ''[[Populus tremula|P. tremula]]'' (common aspen). It is intermediate between its parents, with a thin grey downy coating on the [[leaves]], which are much less deeply lobed than the leaves of ''P. alba''. It is a very vigorous tree with marked [[heterosis|hybrid vigour]], reaching {{Convert|40|m|abbr=off}} tall and with a trunk diameter over {{Convert|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}{{Snd}}much larger than either of its parents. Most trees in [[Horticulture|cultivation]] are male, but female trees occur naturally and some of these are also propagated.<ref name=Rush99/>

==Taxonomy==
In 1789, [[William Aiton]] described the grey poplar as a [[Variety (botany)|variety]] of ''[[Populus alba]]'', ''P. alba'' var. ''canescens''.<ref name=TPL_kew-5004269/> In 1804, [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] raised it to a full species, ''P. canescens''.<ref name=TPL_kew-5000115/> He described differences between the leaves of the two taxa: ''P. alba'' has lobed leaves with snow-white ("''niveus''") undersides, whereas ''P. canescens'' has wavy-edged leaves with hoary ("''incanus''") undersides.<ref name=Smit04/> Later authors sometimes noted the possibility that the grey poplar was a hybrid.<ref name=Phil78/> It is now considered to be a hybrid between ''P. alba'' and ''[[Populus tremula|P. tremula]]'',<ref name=Stac10/> so the scientific name is written with the hybrid symbol.
